comments.author: Frank Berthold
comments.text: 2026-09-05: requirement 3 turns out to carry the mirror of this defect, filed as tla-oljv. Requirement 2 bundles two arms that are both load-bearing, for a reason that measured out to be the load vector. Requirement 3 bundles two conjuncts where one is dead against the declared set. Take them together when either is worked, since the answer to 'what is one property' is the same question both times.

comments.author: Frank Berthold
comments.text:
2026-09-05, from the taste-critic's blind first run, and it is a better diagnosis than central's. The property-count rubric pins the count to INVARIANT plus PROPERTY lines in the reference cfg (V2-PLAN.md:311). A LINE COUNT IS INVARIANT UNDER CONJUNCTION. So any author who needs a smaller number can always get one by joining two obligations with a conjunction, and the dial is gameable by construction rather than by accident. Requirement 2's join is what that bought.

Corpus check from the same run: of 220 configs carrying at least one obligation, 123 sit at two to four and 32 sit at five or more. So four is an ordinary place to stop and five is what about one published config in seven does. Nothing in practice makes five a wall.

Its recommendation, and central agrees: change the rubric rather than the problem. Count an obligation's top-level conjuncts instead of its cfg lines. Splitting the property instead just moves the same squeeze onto the next author, and the split reference measures green at the reference's own 64 distinct states.

comments.author: Frank Berthold
comments.text:
2026-09-05, THIRD instance of the vector authoring the material, from the floor-malting critic, and this one has no artifact-side fix at all.

Rung 5 sits at form left open 0, so the statement hands over every keyword, every formula kind and every subscript for all seven requirements. The author's own step 6 read: 'once the state exists the seven formulas are close to transcription', and all three panel seats put the same requirement under INVARIANT and the other six under PROPERTY, so the spread had to be read off the state instead.

Why it cannot bend on the artifact side: property count 2 is already the rung's single new high, so form 1 would be a second and breach clause (b'). And the count cannot come down either, because band 2 is five to nine obligations and seven requirements plus TypeOK is eight. Reaching band 1 means deleting three requirements.

The critic's point, and I think it is right: band 2's interior is four obligations wide, so any honest set between five and nine spends the rung's entire budget on a number the author had no way to miss. A dimension the plan still marks provisional then gets a veto over where the discrimination lives.

So the count rubric now has two independent complaints against it. It is gameable downward by conjunction, from the bonded-store run, and its bands are wide enough to consume a rung's whole allowance, from this one.

comments.author: Frank Berthold
comments.text:
2026-09-05, FOURTH instance, estate-notice, and this one has measured evidence of the cost.

Requirement 1's two conditions share one config line. Splitting them gives ten lines, which takes property count from band 2 to band 3, and count's running maximum is already 2, so a split puts two dimensions above the maximum and breaches clause (b'). The band is load-bearing.

What the merge costs, measured by the dead-conjunct sweep in the same run: the notice arm reads DEAD against all 36 variants. It is not really dead. S02 distributes while the notice is open, a creditor then lodges because the notice is still open, and the OTHER arm catches it one step later, so no row moves. Split into two lines both are live, S02 lands on the notice line at 2 states and S01 on the other at 4, and TLC names which one failed. That is Lamport's own reason for separate names, Specifying Systems p.259, and this project's own section 3.7 on error location.

So the count rubric now has three complaints. Gameable downward by conjunction (bonded-store). Bands wide enough to eat a rung's whole budget (floor-malting). And here, a merge that costs the learner the diagnosis TLC would otherwise hand them.

Three of the five problems reviewed so far have had their shape set by this dimension.

comments.author: Frank Berthold
comments.text:
2026-09-05, FIFTH instance, river-call, and it is the cleanest demonstration that the dodge works.

The statement closes the requirement list at four and says do not add a fifth. Rule 10 fixes the opening and nothing checks it: S18 opens with every call standing and passes all four lines. Adding a fifth cfg line to pin the opening breaches (b'), measured, since sequence.sh --check reports two dimensions rising at once at position 3.

Now the dodge, measured in the same run. Conjoin the opening check INTO an existing obligation. The cfg still carries four lines, the reference still returns rc=0, and S18 goes from rc=0 to rc=13. The hole closes and the number does not move.

So the band prices the decomposition practice attests, four bundles over disjoint state in 899 obligations, and lets the near-unattested one through for free. The author refused the dodge and wrote the trade down at DESCRIPTION.md:326-330, which is the honest thing and also why the hole is still live.

Four of the five problems reviewed have had their shape set by this dimension. The critic's recommendation on this one is to count named requirements rather than cfg lines, which is the same fix bonded-store's run proposed from the other direction.

comments.author: Frank Berthold
comments.text:
2026-09-05, SIXTH instance, assay-office, and it quantifies the cost.

Six rules ship as three cfg lines. Two obligations each join several rules. Measured: the same content as seven named lines gives IDENTICAL verdicts on all 26 rows, so the join buys nothing except the number. Count moves 4 to 7, which is level 2 and a second new high where the rung's only permitted one is property kind.

The cost, counted: across 9 caught variants the shipped set names 2 causes where the split set names 5. That is Lamport's Specifying Systems p.259 point turned into a number. A named obligation is the checker's label, and merging throws the label away.

Two more sites in the same problem. Dropping TypeOK from the cfg leaves all 26 rows identical, so one of the four counted lines is inert. And a fifth line that would have closed a real hole was priced against the band and refused, recorded at AssayOffice-commented.tla:508.

TALLY. Five problems examined, five had their shape set by this one dimension: bonded-store, river-call, assay-office, floor-malting, estate-notice. Three independent critics reached the same recommendation without seeing each other, count named requirements or top-level conjuncts rather than cfg lines.

This is no longer a defect in a rubric. It is the rubric authoring the material, everywhere it has been looked at.

comments.author: Frank Berthold
comments.text:
2026-09-05, FINAL TALLY. Six problems examined by independent critics. Six had their shape set by a load-vector band.

bonded-store, count. river-call, count. assay-office, count at three separate sites. floor-malting, form. estate-notice, count. herbarium-sheet, form.

Herbarium adds a structural point about the form dimension that the count findings do not reach. Keyword, subscript and statability are three independent decisions stacked into one ordered scale, so K=1 forces an author to take the CHEAPEST of the three. Here that meant handing over both interesting form questions, which rules have no form over the interface and what keyword requirement 7 takes, and keeping only a subscript the neighbouring requirement already answers. The plan already marks this dimension provisional and schedules a re-test at tla-h2cg.5, so splitting it costs a note on that re-test rather than a decision now.

Six for six is not a rubric defect any more.

title: The instance probe decides a package's fate on a text scan, not a parse
description:
`op_body` in `harness/grade.sh` reads a definition by taking its column-1 line and
everything down to the next line that starts in column 1. It is a static text scan,
not a parser, and the implementer said so in a comment above it when it landed at
df5a272.

It became load-bearing in the same commit. The new instance probe decides whether a
reference obligation reads a CONSTANT by looking for a declared constant name inside
that body, and the answer gates whether the package is accepted at all. So a body the
scan reads wrongly is a package wrongly refused, or worse, an obligation the instance
cannot falsify that gets graded anyway.

The assumption holds across every obligations module in the fixture tree today, which
is why the gate is green. It is a convention nothing enforces. A module that puts a
continuation at column 1, or a definition followed by a column-1 comment, would read
short.

Two ways out and I do not have a preference yet. Enforce the convention with a check
that refuses a module the scan cannot read confidently. Or stop scanning and ask SANY,
which already parses these modules for every other purpose.

title: 'State your properties over Observe' has no ruling, and two rungs asked from opposite sides
description:
AUTOFAN-EXCLUDE: a ruling to take once and apply to every shipped rung, attended.

Every v2 problem tells the learner to state the requirements as formulas over Observe. Nothing says whether that binds the text or the meaning. Bonded store and laytime both raised it at step 6, from opposite directions, and the herbarium and estate-notice panels are living with the same ambiguity by luck rather than by rule.

The two readings. On the text reading, a formula has to mention Observe and its field names, so a seat that renames the fields into its own variables has not done what was asked even if the formula says the same thing. On the meaning reading, any formula that constrains the same behaviours passes, and Observe is a specification of what the properties may depend on rather than a syntax to copy.

Where it bites hardest is a rung whose Observe is the identity on the state. There the grading fixes the field names anyway, so nothing a seat wrote was unsound under either reading, and the spread rule then reads three converged representations as trivial or leaking when they are neither. The extractor's eighth triple narrows the rule for that case. Floor malting is the contrast: same shape, same representation level, real spread, because its state is not the interface.

Take the ruling once, write it into V2-PLAN section 2.5 or section 6 rather than into a rung, and say which of the two it is. Then say what the spread rule does on a rung where the interface is the identity, since the current rule gives the wrong answer there.

title: A re-dispatched panel seat inherits its killed run's artifacts
description:
AUTOFAN-EXCLUDE: process fix to the step 6 panel brief and its staging, attended.

A session rate limit killed two of rung 6's three seats partway through on 2026-09-05. Both were dispatched again into the same staging directory under ~/tla-puzzles-panel/<slug>/p<N>/, which still held the killed run's module, cfg, replay tree and logs.

The two seats handled it differently and the difference was invisible until they reported. One inherited a finished spec it had never watched itself write, disclosed that in a provenance note, and declined to give an attempt count rather than invent one. The other moved the leftovers to _preexisting/ unread and rebuilt from scratch, so its one attempt is real.

The cost is the attempts column, which is one of the four things the spread rule reads. A seat that reports a clean first-try solve over an inherited spec is not measuring what the column is for, and nothing in the brief or the staging tells the reader which happened. Here it surfaced only because the seat was honest.

Two fixes and they are independent. The staging should be cleared or the seat directory renamed before any re-dispatch, which is central's job and belongs in the panel dispatch step. And the seat brief should carry the instruction the honest seat invented: if the directory holds anything beyond the staged learner files, move it aside unread and say so.

title: vacuity.sh's dead-action probe is blind to a single-label PlusCal either
description:
Rung 1's verifier (tla-h2cg.7, authoring/bonded-store/reports/step2-variants.md) found that a PlusCal spec with one label and an `either` produces coverage rows all named `Next`, so `harness/vacuity.sh --expect-actions Next` returns NON_VACUOUS rc=0 on variant S25, which removes a whole branch. 5.3's dead-action predicate reads action names, and at this shape every branch shares one. The probe is blind for every shape B problem at the floor's altitude, which is exactly where a removed branch is the natural seeded bug.

Two routes: teach the probe to read per-branch coverage from the `either` (TLC's coverage output names the line, which is enough to tell branches apart), or have the verifier brief say the dead-action probe needs a distinct-count comparison at this shape. The second is what the rung 1 report did by hand.

title: 01-custody ships as first contact, and its author suspected it was too hard
description:
Frank, 2026-09-04, having finished learntla core and looking at seat 01 for the first time: does this look like a first model?

It does not, and the author said so before it shipped.

`authoring/custody/reports/step4-screens.md:173`:

> I suspect P1 runs past the 20 to 40 minute target for a first-contact learner. Ten properties is a lot of rendering. **If that is wrong, the blind panel will say so cheaply.**

The blind panel is three agents already fluent in TLA+. The only timing it reported is p2's, at 40 seconds (`step6-spread.md:56`). So the panel measured the machine cost and could not have measured the thing the author was worried about. That is `tla-rrwl` one layer up: a suspicion deferred to an instrument structurally unable to answer it.

## What seat 01 asks of someone who has just finished the grammar

- Invent the state layout for a 14-day two-party arrangement from nine prose rules, with three independent sources of steps (A, B, and days beginning unprompted).
- Establish TEN properties: invariants, three action properties, and one liveness property needing fairness.
- Against roughly 100,000 distinct states at 2 to 3 minutes per run.

Against a background of 10-to-15-minute chapter drills that target one construct each and top out at five per set.

## The trap, which is good and badly sited

`Observe.custodian` is a function from day to parent, so the interface suggests modelling custody as a mutable function and reassigning entries. Property 3, "a day's custodian changes at most once over the window", is brutal that way: it is a fact about history, not about a state.

The reference keeps a SET of swapped days and derives `custodian`. Then at-most-one-flip falls out, because a set that only grows cannot flip a day twice.

That is a real modelling insight and the screens report names it as the intended difficulty. It is also the kind of insight you have after a few models rather than during your first, and the problem's own observation interface points away from it.

## Immediate mitigation

`03-buyclub` estimates itself at 20 to 40 minutes in its first three lines. `01-custody` gives no time estimate at all, only a warning that runs take minutes. Suggest buyclub as first contact and custody once a model exists.

The seat order came from the diagonal walk, which serves interleaving. Interleaving is about not repeating a task shape and says nothing about ramp, so nothing in the design requires the hardest column-A problem to be first.

The general version of this is filed separately as the difficulty-progression bead.

title: Eight chapters talk about console output the harness deletes
description:
Found by the `tla-jb7f.27` cold-solve reviewer against ch.12 and confirmed cross-cutting by central.

`harness/verdict.sh:346` sends all TLC output to a file inside its scratch directory. When the caller passes neither `--log` nor `--scratch`, `CLEAN_SCRATCH=1` and the EXIT trap at `:292-307` removes the directory. The exercise text has not caught up. Only ch.02, ch.04 and ch.10 mention `--log` or `--scratch`. Nine chapters talk about output the learner cannot see.

Two severities, and they want different fixes.

**Harmless but confusing, four chapters.** ch.04, ch.06, ch.07 and ch.08 say "ignore the console noise above it". There is none, so a learner scrolls up looking for something that was never printed and concludes they ran the command wrong. ch.05, ch.09, ch.11 and ch.13 carry milder phrasings of the same. This is template-inherited: the sentence is the same in every chapter that has it.

**Blocking, one site, and it is already filed under `tla-jb7f.27`'s repair.** `exercises/ch12/EXERCISES.md:277` says "Read the trace and check which winch stalled", which is exercise 4's own insight and cannot be done.

I think the right fix is at the template rather than per chapter: document `--log` once in the shared How-to-run section, and delete the ignore-the-console sentence everywhere, since it exists only to explain noise the harness no longer produces. ch.02, ch.04 and ch.10 already carry a `--log` line, so there is a form to copy rather than invent.

Worth noting for prioritisation: Frank is at ch.10 and has worked ch.02 through ch.09, so he has already met four of these sentences.

title: Two accuracy gaps in the ch.12 cheat sheet, found by authoring against it
description:
Both found by the `tla-jb7f.27` author while building exercises from the sheet, which is the pass the cross-sheet review cannot do because it reads rather than uses.

**Theme 4's quoted error is truncated.** The sheet quotes TLC's incomplete-next-state message. TLC actually says `...by action Refill of the next-state relation. The following variable is not defined: rows.` The sheet drops both the action name and the variable name. A learner matching the sheet's text against their own output will not find it. Theme 5's quote was checked and is verbatim, so this is one site rather than a habit.

**`\E` over a temporal formula is undocumented.** `\E w \in S : WF_vars(A(w))` model-checks on this build and returns `LIVENESS_VIOLATION` rather than being refused. The sheet says nothing about it, and ch.12 exercise 4 depends on the behaviour. Recorded as a `bd remember` too, since it affects any spec quantifying fairness over a set of processes, not only the exercises.

title: ASSUME in a module reached through INSTANCE is never checked
description:
Found by the `tla-jb7f.28` author while authoring the ch.13 module exercises, and reproduced independently by central.

A module's `ASSUME` is not checked when the module is reached through `INSTANCE`. Minimal probe, on the pinned build:

    ---- MODULE Band ----
    EXTENDS Naturals
    CONSTANTS Lo, Hi
    ASSUME Lo <= Hi
    Width == Hi - Lo
    ====

    ---- MODULE Main ----
    EXTENDS Naturals
    VARIABLE x
    UnusedBand == INSTANCE Band WITH Lo <- 99, Hi <- 1
    Init == x = 0
    Next == x' = x
    Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_x
    ====

`tlc -config Main.cfg Main.tla` exits 0. It parses `Band.tla`, reports "Model checking completed. No error has been found", and prints no assumption message of any kind. `99 <= 1` is false.

The consequence is the sentence worth remembering: a library that guards its constants with `ASSUME` guards nothing once anybody instantiates it. That is exactly the situation ch.13 teaches, since the whole chapter is about `INSTANCE ... WITH` supplying an imported module's constants.

Mutant C4 of the ch.13 set is inert for this reason and is documented as such, so the set records the behaviour rather than depending on it.

I do not know whether this is the language or the build, and that distinction decides what the fix is. If it is the language, the exercises and any future module-using reference need to stop relying on `ASSUME` for cross-module constant validation, and say so. If it is the build, it is worth reporting upstream alongside the TLAiBench defects in `tla-sgc`.

The check to run first is `Specifying Systems` on whether `INSTANCE` is specified to check assumptions, then the same probe on a second tla2tools build. Note that the project's canonical build is pinned to a mirror now (`tla-yvky`), so a second build means fetching one deliberately rather than trusting a tag.

Files: exercises/ch13/reports/authoring.md

RED: INVARIANT: a spec instantiating a module whose ASSUME its WITH substitution violates is either refused by TLC, or documented in the ch.13 material as unchecked.

comments.author: Frank Berthold
comments.text:
The ch.13 cold-solve reviewer ran the contrast the original report was missing, and central reproduced both halves. The scoping is sharper than the bead first said.

An `ASSUME` in the ROOT module IS checked:

    ---- MODULE Direct ----
    ASSUME 99 <= 1
    ====

    rc=10, "Error: Assumption line 4, col 8 to line 4, col 14 of module Direct is false."

The same assumption reached through `INSTANCE ... WITH` is not, at rc=0 with no message.

So this is not "ASSUME is unreliable". It is specifically that instantiation does not carry the assumption, which is a narrower and more reportable claim. That matters for the language-versus-build question: a build bug would more likely break both, and a language rule about `INSTANCE` semantics would break exactly this one.

Second-order consequence worth chasing: the delivered ch.05 cheat sheet tells the learner `ASSUME` "documents and enforces valid constant values before a run starts" (`ch05.md:47`). That is true of the root module and false through `INSTANCE`, and ch.13 is the chapter where a learner first meets the second case. The ch.05 sheet is not wrong for ch.05, so the fix is a boundary note rather than a correction.

title: CI installs the toolchain by hand instead of running scripts/setup
description:
The `Install TLA+ tools` step in `.github/workflows/verify-puzzles.yml` runs its own `curl`, writes its own `tlc`/`pcal` wrappers, and asserts the version in a separate step. `scripts/setup` does all four of those things, and it's the copy that `harness/test-toolchain-pin.sh` actually exercises.

So CI runs an install path no test covers, next to a tested one it ignores. `tla-yvky` closed the immediate hole by teaching the workflow to check the digest too, which means the check now exists twice and has to stay in step twice.

Fix: have the workflow call `bash scripts/setup` and drop its hand-rolled install. The awkward part is `$GITHUB_PATH` — the workflow appends `$HOME/bin` to it so later steps resolve `tlc`, and `scripts/setup` only warns when `$HOME/bin` isn't on `PATH`. So the step keeps one line of its own after delegating.

I think this is worth doing but it isn't urgent. The duplication is honest today because `tla-yvky` left both copies naming the same pinned digest, and `scripts/cibuild` phase 1 cross-checks that they agree. What it buys is that CI would run the path the test suite gates, instead of a parallel one that only drifts when somebody forgets.

title: Lane A is §3.7's control arm, not its worst arm — and §3.7 overreaches its citation
description:
Central filed a handoff hole saying Lane A might be §3.7's worst arm (natural-language description
hints, below control, most demoralizing). **The research audit says that framing is wrong, and the
correction matters.**

The RCT's three arms were hints delivered DURING solving, ABOUT the learner's own error. Lane A's
commented reference differs on all three defining properties: post-attempt not mid-impasse; about
the REFERENCE's decisions not the learner's error; elective reading not interruptive feedback. The
demoralization finding attached to being told in prose what is wrong with your work while stuck.
**Lane A is not the NL arm. In the study's terms it is the CONTROL arm.**

So the cost is not "below control". It is forfeiting the one arm that worked, roughly a 60%
task-completion gain.

**But there is a real compound nobody had written down.** With no grader, the only verdict channel
on Frank's attempt is his own comparison of it to the reference. That is reference-comparison
grading — §3.5's banned method — performed by the least-equipped grader available, in a domain
chosen under §3.10 precisely so he lacks the schema to adjudicate, where §3.5's own data predicts a
correct-but-different form looks wrong most of the time (oracle ranks #1 for 33%, absent in 18.6%).
The output, "mine looks wrong, this felt bad", is what §7.1 says is a reliable AMBIGUITY signal and
an unreliable DIFFICULTY signal. So mis-graded self-comparison masquerades as bug reports and feeds
§7.1's fix-the-broken loop with false positives.

**Zero-cost partial fix:** ship the author's `alternatives.md` (the representations considered and
rejected) WITH the commentary rather than keeping it author-only. It is the one existing artifact
that shows Frank the space of correct-but-different.

**Separately, §3.7 overreaches its own citation.** Its last line is "Nothing improved retention", so
the positive result is an in-practice PERFORMANCE result. By §7.2's own standard, performance during
practice is an unreliable index of learning. §3.7 is sound as harm-avoidance and as UX; as a claim
that location feedback TEACHES, it exceeds what the study shows. The invariant policing feedback
quality rests on the metric class the project disavows.

title: Difficulty verdicts do not record which models produced them
description:
Every difficulty judgment this project makes runs through blind solvers, and §2.1's target —
problems that admit real modeling choice — is measured by their spread. Nothing records which
models produced a verdict.

That matters two ways.

**A verdict from one family is a verdict about that family.** The Stage 3 pilot's step 6 used three
instances of one model and returned byte-identical answers. The mixed-panel re-run
(`pilot/reports/step6-mixed-panel.md`) showed the content convergence was real and not a panel
artifact — but it also showed that a three-instance single-model panel returned 0 in 3 on a defect
that the six-critic mixed panel caught at 1 in 6.

**Calibration goes stale silently.** A problem tuned to be hard for today's models may be trivial
for next year's, and nothing in the pipeline would notice. The `tla-03d2` research reached the same
conclusion about its recall probe and prescribed the fix there: record the model id and the date
with the verdict.

Asks:

- Record panel composition — model ids, count per model, date — alongside every step-6 result and
  every difficulty verdict.
- Prefer mixed panels. The measured reason is not that content diverges, because it did not. It is
  that depth of justification does, and depth is what column C grades.
- Re-run the panel when the model set changes, and treat a verdict older than the current model set
  as unverified rather than as passing.

title: grade.sh resolves REPO_ROOT from the caller's cwd, so another repo's harness can be loaded
description:
`grade.sh:196` resolves the repo root from the CALLER's cwd:

    REPO_ROOT=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null || echo ".")

and then loads `$REPO_ROOT/harness/verdict.sh` and `$REPO_ROOT/harness/Gate.tla` from it.

Run from outside any repo it dies loudly — `HARNESS ERROR: missing the verdict channel:
./harness/verdict.sh`, rc=4, measured. That case is fine.

**Run from inside a DIFFERENT git repo, it silently picks up that repo's `harness/verdict.sh` and
`harness/Gate.tla`.** The verdict channel and the gate module are the two things the whole grading
architecture rests on, and both would come from somewhere nobody chose.

This is bead `tla-1hf` in the mirror direction. There, `scripts/gen-curriculum-map.sh` hardcoded a
`cd` to the repo root, so running it from a worktree wrote into the MAIN checkout. The rule that
came out of it is in `.claude/rules/dispatched-agents.md`: **if a script resolves a repo root,
resolve it from `${BASH_SOURCE[0]}`, never from a literal path** — and, this bead adds, never from
the caller's cwd either.

`scripts/cibuild:43-45` already does it correctly and is the model.

Worth checking the other harness scripts for the same shape while fixing this one.

title: grade.sh appends its constants.cfg unvalidated, the third site of one class
description:
Three harness components build a `.cfg` from a caller-supplied fragment. Two of them now refuse a
directive in that fragment. `grade.sh` does not.

- `refinement.sh --constants` — guard existed but was line-anchored while TLC's parser is
  token-oriented, so `(* c *) SYMMETRY Perms` walked past it. Hardened in `tla-nesz`.
- `seeded-bugs.sh constants.cfg` — validated from the start, added in `tla-40y`, refusing a
  directive as `MATRIX_MALFORMED`.
- **`grade.sh constants.cfg` — appended verbatim, no validation.** `grade.sh:361` is
  `[ -n "$CONST_FRAG" ] && cat "$CONST_FRAG"`, straight into every generated judge `.cfg`.

Two independent agents found the first two on the same day without knowing about each other, which
is why I think this is a class rather than three bugs.

**What it costs here, and it is not the SYMMETRY story.** grade.sh emits `INVARIANT
GRADE_OBLIGATION`, and symmetry reduction on pure invariant checking is sound, so §10's temporal
hazard does not bite directly. The live one is a smuggled second `INVARIANT`: grade.sh reads rc=12
as "the obligation was UNMET", so a second invariant firing is misattributed to the obligation
under test. A `CONSTRAINT` is the other direction — it truncates the reachable space and can turn
an UNMET into a MET.

Threat model is weaker than for the other two, because the reference package is harness-owned
rather than submission-owned. So this is an author-error trap, not an attack surface. That is
still worth closing: §5.7's whole posture is that the `.cfg` stays harness-owned precisely so
grading cannot be weakened, and an author who puts one wrong line in `constants.cfg` gets silently
wrong grades rather than an error.

Fix: reuse `seeded-bugs.sh`'s validator rather than writing a third one. Strip `\*` comments,
match keywords as tokens anywhere rather than line-anchored, refuse anything that is not a
`CONSTANT` or `CONSTANTS` assignment.

Worth checking at the same time whether a fourth site exists. `vacuity.sh` has no constants
channel today, which may itself be a gap, since it cannot drive a parameterized spec either.

title: refinement.sh reports a real refinement failure as SAFETY_VIOLATION
description:
`harness/refinement.sh` RUN A routes rc=13 to `REFINEMENT_VIOLATED` and everything else to a
catch-all that emits the raw verdict token. Central checked the common cases during the pilot and
they route correctly: implied-init and implied-action obligations both exit 13, and so does a
broken fairness conjunct.

The `tla-94n` worker found the case the corrected row-13 predicts. **An abstract spec whose own
`Spec` formula carries a safety-shaped temporal conjunct exits 12.**

Measured: `ASpec == AInit /\ [][ANext]_a /\ [](AHot => []AHot)`, concrete violating the third
conjunct, gives rc=12 `SAFETY_VIOLATION` with `Error: Temporal property Refines was violated`.

So a genuine refinement failure is reported as `SAFETY_VIOLATION` rather than
`REFINEMENT_VIOLATED`, and a caller branching on the token sees a safety violation with no
refinement in it.

This follows directly from `tla-94n`: 12 and 13 split on the shape of the formula, not on the
`.cfg` keyword. A refinement `PROPERTY` inherits whatever shapes the abstract `Spec` carries, and
a `[](P => []P)` conjunct in an abstract spec is ordinary rather than exotic.

Not fixed at source because it sat outside the `tla-94n` worker's footprint, which was right.

The fix needs care rather than a second `12)` arm: rc=12 from RUN A could be a refinement
violation or a genuine invariant violation in the concrete spec, and the exit code alone does not
separate them. RUN A declares no `INVARIANT` today, which may be enough to make the case
unambiguous. Check that before assuming it.

title: test-pipefail.sh cannot see workflow YAML, where the hazard was live
description:
`harness/test-pipefail.sh` bans `| grep -q`, `| grep -m` and `| head` across the tree, selecting
files by shebang rather than by extension so that files which do not exist yet are covered the
moment they land. GitHub workflow YAML has no shebang and no `.sh` suffix, so it is invisible to
the scanner.

That is not hypothetical. `.github/workflows/verify-puzzles.yml` carried three hits, one of them
the load-bearing toolchain-version assertion, and the workflow had been failing since 2026-08-06
without anyone seeing it. `tla-1qn` fixed the site. The gate that exists to catch this class
structurally could not see the file.

The argument for widening is that `run:` blocks in this repo set `set -euo pipefail` themselves,
so the hazard is live there in exactly the form the scanner was written for.

The `tla-1qn` worker measured the change and did not make it, correctly, since widening a gate's
selection is its own bead. What it costs: one entry in `SCAN_ROOTS` (currently `harness scripts
chapter`, `test-pipefail.sh:184`), a selector clause admitting `.github/workflows/*.yml`
(`:206-214`), and a `check_root .github 1` floor. It also confirmed the whole-line comment strip
at `:298` correctly swallows documentation that mentions the banned idiom, so the new
explanatory comment in the workflow will not self-trip the scanner.

title: §9.8's recognition stop asks about the problem, not the mechanism
description:
§9.8 tells a blind agent: "if you recognize this as a known published problem, say so immediately
and stop."

On the pilot one critic answered that question explicitly — "I do not recognize this as a known
published problem, it reads as a synthetic puzzle, so I proceeded" — and then, at the end,
identified the system as two-phase commit.

All three critics recognized 2PC. All three noticed while reading Rule 3, before opening the
spec. None stopped, and none was wrong not to. The problem IS synthetic and unpublished. The
control asks about provenance when the risk is mechanism.

§5.7 already screens mechanism rather than name, and the survey drawer says outright that name
novelty is not mechanism novelty. §9.8's stop condition never got the same treatment.

Fix: ask both, and treat them differently. Stop on a recognized published problem. Report a
recognized mechanism without stopping, because that is measurement rather than disqualification.
Asking it last leaks nothing, which the pilot confirmed on all three.

title: §6 never says which artifacts a blind agent may see
description:
Step 4 produced four files in one directory: the statement, the deficient spec, the answer key and
the author's screen answers. `ANSWER-KEY.md` opens with "Never show this to a critic" and sat in
the directory a critic reads. `screens.md` names both seeded gaps by rule number.

Central caused it by telling the statement author where to write, and agent D caught it. A step-6
brief saying "read the statement directory" would have handed three blind critics the answers, and
the file's own warning line is exactly the instruction isolation §6b.1 exists to reject.

Fixed for the pilot structurally rather than by instruction. The answer key and screens moved out
of the tree, and each critic got its own directory outside `pilot/` holding exactly three files.

§6 should say this rather than leaving it to whoever writes the brief. Every step that dispatches
a blind agent needs a named artifact set, not a directory, and author-only outputs belong
somewhere a blind agent has no path to. Stage 4's `tla-practice` / `tla-answers` split is the same
rule one level up, and §6 needs its own version because the pilot runs before Stage 4 exists.

title: PUZZLE-SCREEN.md Q2 is calibrated for column A, so column C can never pass it
description:
Q2 asks whether the legal moves are given by the domain or decided by the learner. A critique
problem hands the learner an action set by construction, twice over: in the statement's rules and
again in the spec being critiqued. So a column-C problem answers Q2 "given" every time, which is
the puzzle answer, and it is structural rather than a wording defect.

Agent C hit this on the pilot and reported it instead of rewording around it. Its reading, which I
find persuasive: a column-C form of Q2 would ask whether the learner has to decide what a
REQUIREMENT is, which for the pilot is yes. The modeling judgment moves from "what are the
actions" to "which rules are state predicates, which are transition properties, and which the
observation vocabulary can carry at all".

The tally rule fires at three puzzle answers across Q2 to Q8, so one structural puzzle answer
doesn't sink a column-C problem today. It does mean the score is off by one for an entire column,
and Stage 5 authors eight of them.

Files: harness/PUZZLE-SCREEN.md
notes:
WIDEN from Q2 to Q1 AND Q2. Agent D's independent screen (pilot step 5) found Q1 has the same defect: its system column reads 'the actions themselves', which column C can never claim for the same structural reason Q2 can't read 'decided'. A critique problem is handed an action set twice over.

Agent D also sharpened the diagnosis on Q2. It is not merely structurally given — the pilot's PROBLEM.md enumerates every action in prose as well, so delete the attached spec and the statement alone is still a complete action set. Doubly given, not structurally given.

The fix both readings point at is the same: the rubric needs a requirement-centric answer pair for Q1 and Q2, not a footnote on one row. For column C the question is whether the learner must decide what a REQUIREMENT is, which for the pilot is yes.

title: §6's pipeline has no repair loop when a gate comes back red
description:
§6's pipeline is eight steps and four gates with no arrow back. Step 2's gate reads "all green".
The pilot's step 2 came back PARTIAL, five of eleven adversarial variants uncaught, and the plan
says nothing about what happens next.

The gap isn't theoretical. §9.5 tells the verifier "do not fix anything; report only", which is
right, so the pipeline needs a named repair step and a re-verification, and it needs to say who
does each. Stage 5 authors 12 problems in a batch and this will come up every time.

Central resolved it for the pilot by dispatching a third agent to repair against the verifier's
findings and re-run the frozen variant set. That shape is worth keeping, because it holds the
separation: the verifier authors the variants adversarially, the variants freeze, and a repairer
who didn't author them has to make them go red. The test set doesn't move under the person trying
to pass it.

comments.author: Frank Berthold
comments.text:
Raising to P1 on 2026-09-03. This is the mechanism failure behind every uncaught variant in batch 1, and batch 1 is what Frank is working now.

The authors' own step-2 numbers, all five problems, none repaired:

| problem | result |
|---|---|
| custody | 19 caught, 7 uncaught of 26 |
| seedlib | 36 of 47 caught, 11 uncaught, **gate verdict RED** |
| consign | 18 caught, 6 uncaught |
| buyclub | V24, V25, V26 uncaught at rc 0 |
| qsl | S16, S17, S18 uncaught at rc 0 |

`find authoring -iname "*repair*" -o -iname "*step2b*" -o -iname "*step3*"` returns nothing. Each problem has step2, step4, step5 and step6 reports and no repair. So §9.5 forbade the verifier from fixing, §9.5b named a repairer, and the repairer never ran on any of the five.

custody states its own consequence plainly: "So Rules 3 and 4 are ungraded as things stand." V08 and V10 generate 496,735 states and 102,460 distinct, the reference's numbers to the digit, because `Scheduled` is read by both the mutation and every obligation that mentions the schedule. The yardstick moves with the model.

Two things keep this from being worse than it is, and both belong in the record.

First, the classes matter more than the counts. custody sorts its seven into three classes and says only one is a hole in the obligation set. An uncaught variant means a defective submission would pass, not that the statement is unsound. Steps 4, 5 and 6 covered statement soundness and passed.

Second, the reports are honest and were written before the runs, with a frozen matrix. The measurement discipline worked exactly as designed. What is missing is only the arrow back.

The learner-facing consequence is the one that raises the priority: the answer to "how do I know I got this right" is "the grader tells you", and the grader has a measured, documented, unrepaired hole in every problem of the batch.

My previous comment said "no repair pass ever ran on any of the five" and raised this to P1. The repairs are appended as `RESULTS-2B` sections inside each problem's own `step2-variants.md`, which is the protocol §9.5b actually specifies. Searching filenames for something recorded in-file is a bad check, and it returned a clean-looking zero rather than an error.

- `V2-PLAN.md:1383` — `### 9.5b Reference repairer (step 2b)`, the brief itself
- `V2-PLAN.md:933` — "the pipeline now names the repair step, the repairer"
- `V2-PLAN.md:955` — "central dispatches the repair there rather than reflexively one step back"

The actual post-repair state of batch 1:

| problem | verdict | remaining uncaught |
|---|---|---|
| buyclub | GREEN | 7, all expected, structural causes named; the author argues AGAINST adding obligations |
| consign | GREEN | 5, four declared uncatchable plus one inert |
| qsl | — | 3, "all structurally uncatchable" |

title: A violated PROPERTY can exit 12, so verdict.sh's row-13 gloss misleads
description:
Measured on tla2tools v1.8.0, each property declared ALONE with no invariant in the .cfg:

- `[](P => []P)` violated exits 12, token SAFETY_VIOLATION
- `[][A]_vars` violated exits 13, token LIVENESS_VIOLATION

Row 13 of verdict.sh's table reads `PROPERTY violated (incl. refinement, §5.4)`. That holds for
action properties and fails for the temporal shape above. The sharper consequence runs the other
way: rc=12 doesn't imply an INVARIANT was violated, and the probe showing it declared no
invariant at all.

Refinement is not affected. Implied-init and implied-action violations both exit 13, so
harness/refinement.sh:524 routes correctly. I checked that on purpose, because the lone `13)`
branch there would have misrouted a real refinement failure into the catch-all.

Where it bites today is the learner-facing token. §3.7 makes feedback error location, and
SAFETY_VIOLATION on a failed temporal property points someone at the wrong thing.

Where it bites harder is tla-59s. If grade.sh grows temporal obligations it emits PROPERTY, and
an UNMET obligation then arrives as 13 where grade.sh expects 12, which routes to HARNESS_ERROR.
Fix this row first.

Probe kept at scratchpad rcprobe/PropShape.tla with two single-property configs. Reproduces in
about two seconds.

title: §5.2's grading engine can't grade a temporal obligation
description:
grade.sh generates `SPECIFICATION Spec / INVARIANT <op>(Observe)` for all three suites
(harness/grade.sh:356-357, mechanism table at :131-150). Obligations are `Req_*(o)` over one
observation record, variable-free by design so either spec can EXTEND the module. There's no
primed state and no pair of successive observations, so an obligation relating two states can't
be written at all.

That rules out a class of requirement, not an edge case. Any lifecycle system has rules shaped
"when X happens, Y must be cleared", and those are about transitions. Task shape B asks the
learner to write the property given a spec. §3.9 wants a violating trace with every property,
and a trace is a behaviour.

Concrete instance from the tla-kl5.11 pilot. The municipal-permit-review reference states rule 3
as `AmendmentClearsApprovals == [][ (amendments' # amendments) => (Observe'.approvedBy = {}) ]_vars`.
Agent A established it has no invariant form under the fixed `Observe`. A spec that amends
without clearing leaves stale "approved" entries, so `approvedBy` still reads full and every
invariant passes. Measured rc=13 with no invariant firing. Version-stamping would make it a
state fact, and it was rejected on separate grounds recorded in the reference's alternatives
note.

Two ways out, and I lean to the first:

1. Let `Req_*` take two records, emit a boxed action.
2. Keep it state-only and say so in §5.2.

Option 1 needs the exit-code row fixed first, because a violated action obligation exits 13 and
grade.sh reads 12 as UNMET. Option 2 is honest but narrows what a problem can ask a learner for.

The pilot isn't blocked. It proceeds with a state-expressible primary gap, which the unanimity
requirement supplies.

Files: harness/grade.sh, V2-PLAN.md
notes:
REFINEMENT from the pilot's step 2, and it matters for whoever picks this up: the amendment rule
has TWO independent blockers, and closing the one in the title does not close the other.

1. grade.sh is state-predicate-only. That's the title finding.
2. The fixed `Observe` exposes no amendment count, so an amendment is not observable at the graded
   interface at all.

Even with temporal obligations landed, rule 3 stays ungradable under this operator, because
`AmendmentClearsApprovals` reaches for the raw `amendments` variable rather than a field of
`Observe`. §3.3 says grading keys off Observe and never raw state, so as written that property
could not be a graded obligation regardless of the channel.

Agent B's v09 variant is the sharp instance. Freeze the amendment counter and the property goes
vacuous, since it's guarded by `amendments' # amendments`. Nothing in the graded interface can see
the difference.

Adding an `amendments` field to Observe is the obvious repair and central considered it during the
pilot, then left it. It's legitimate (a revision count is an observable fact about the permit
process, not a representation choice) but it buys no gate improvement until this bead lands,
because "an amendment increments the count" is still temporal. Recorded so the option isn't
re-derived from scratch.

title: §6's pilot pipeline never says who authors the seeded variants
description:
§9.5 tells the reference verifier to run each 'seeded-broken variant supplied' and confirm rc=12. Nothing upstream supplies them. §9.4 gives agent A three deliverables and variants aren't among them, and §5.5 describes the matrix without naming an author. Step 2 has a gate it can't run.

Whoever writes the variants must not be whoever wrote the invariant under test. The matrix asks whether a property ever says no, and an author who writes both tends to write variants their own invariant already catches. That's the self-verification trap the tla-kl5.2 wave was set up to break.

Resolved for the pilot by having agent B author the variants adversarially and then run the matrix, since agent A wrote the invariant. I think that pairing belongs in §6 and §9.5 rather than being re-decided per problem, because Stage 5 authors 12 problems in one batch and the decision won't survive being made twelve times.

Found running the tla-kl5.11 pilot.

title: Gate the 'verdict.sh is the sole TLC entry point' invariant instead of remembering it
description:
The `tla-kl5.3` KG extraction (2026-08-07) declined to encode one relationship as a triple and
noted another was better expressed as a gate. Both are worth acting on.

**1. Make "verdict.sh is the sole TLC entry point" a GATE, not a fact to remember.**

Every harness component routes its TLC invocations through `harness/verdict.sh`, which holds the
canonical flags (`-workers 1`, `-noGenerateSpecTE`, `-metadir`) and the rc→token map:
`grade.sh`, `vacuity.sh`, `refinement.sh`, `seeded-bugs.sh`, and now `scripts/verify-puzzle.sh`.
The extractor verified it holds today — `grep -ln "java -" harness/*.sh` returns nothing.

**But nothing enforces it.** A future component that shells out to `java -cp ... tlc2.TLC`
directly would silently lose `-workers 1` (making counterexamples nondeterministic), lose the
corrected rc table, and re-introduce exactly the stdout-classification this project spent
`tla-syn` removing. That is a correctness invariant depending on human memory, which
gate-don't-advise says must not happen.

Add an assertion — `harness/test-pipefail.sh` already scans by shebang and walks the tree, so it
is the natural host, or a sibling check in `scripts/test`. Exempt `verdict.sh` itself. Note
`comment-gate.sh` and `screen.sh` are legitimately NOT in the set: they use "verdict" as a common
noun and never run TLC, so the assertion is about who launches TLC, not who says "verdict".

**2. `harness/grade.sh:407 token_for()` is a partial second copy of the rc→token map.**
Already filed as part of `tla-6nt`; noting the overlap so the two are not fixed twice. A single
source would make check 1 easier to state.

**3. Deliberately NOT encoded, and worth preserving as a judgement:** the extractor left the
SIGPIPE hazard and the rc=75/rc=14 findings out of the KG on the grounds that each is already
enforced by a gate (`test-pipefail.sh` scans unwritten files; the rc facts are fixture-asserted),
so a triple would duplicate a working enforcement. **If either gate is ever weakened, those facts
need somewhere else to live.** That is the trigger to revisit, not a reason to add them now.

Files: harness/test-pipefail.sh, scripts/test
acceptance_criteria: An assertion fails if any harness/scripts component launches TLC without going through verdict.sh; verdict.sh itself exempt.

title: Follow-ups from tla-i9m: stale rc comments, a duplicated token map, and a fixture pair that doesn't isolate its claim
description:
Three consequences of `tla-i9m` that its worker correctly reported rather than editing out of
footprint, plus one methodology fix.

title: scripts/setup fails at the pip step — Debian PEP 668 externally-managed-environment
description:
`bash scripts/setup` completes its TLA+ toolchain half and then **fails at the pip step**:

    error: externally-managed-environment
    ... If you wish to install a non-Debian-packaged Python package, create a virtual
    environment using python3 -m venv ...
    setup: ERROR — pip install failed

This is Debian/Ubuntu PEP 668. `pip install -r docs-requirements.txt` into the system interpreter
is refused by design on this platform, so `scripts/setup` cannot succeed on a fresh box here.

Found 2026-08-07 running setup for real during tla-wl7. The jar install runs first and completed,
so the toolchain pin landed — but the script exits non-zero, which means anyone following the
documented setup path sees a failure, and `scripts/cibuild` phase ordering may inherit it.

OPTIONS, needs a decision rather than a default:
  (a) Create and use a project venv (`.venv/`), and have `server`/`deploy`/`cibuild` use its
      interpreter. Most correct, most moving parts, and it changes what `package_manager: pip`
      in the constitution means.
  (b) `pipx` for the mkdocs toolchain — it is an application, not a library, so pipx is arguably
      the right tool. Does not help if a plugin needs to be importable alongside.
  (c) `--break-system-packages`. Works, and is exactly what the constitution's `forbidden:` list
      exists to prohibit if anyone cares. Do not pick this silently.
  (d) Detect PEP 668 and degrade: skip the pip step with a clear message naming the fix, so the
      toolchain half still succeeds cleanly. Smallest change; leaves docs deps to the human.

CHECK FIRST whether the docs toolchain is even missing here — `mkdocs` may already be installed
system-wide, in which case the step is a no-op on this machine and the bug only bites a fresh
one. That changes the urgency but not the correctness.

Note this also affects `.claude/project-constitution.md`, which records `package_manager: pip`.
Whichever option wins, the constitution's rationale comment should say why.

Files: scripts/setup, .claude/project-constitution.md
acceptance_criteria: scripts/setup exits 0 on this machine and on a fresh Debian box; the chosen approach is recorded in the constitution's package_manager rationale.

title: gen-curriculum-map.sh hardcodes an absolute cd into the main checkout — worktree leak
description:
`scripts/gen-curriculum-map.sh:5` is:

dispatched worker runs — it writes `CURRICULUM_MAP.md` into the main working tree instead of the
